Core Starsim has the networks most models need: random contacts (`ss.RandomNet`), partnerships (`ss.DegreeNet`, `ss.SexualNet`), mother and child (`ss.PrenatalNet` and its relatives), mixing pools, and contact matrices; they, and how to write a network of your own, are on [Contact networks](populations_networks.qmd). The Starsim library (`import starsim.library as ssl`; see [Library: diseases](library_diseases.qmd) for what the library is) has eight more, for households and other clusters, for space, and for theoretical work:

| Class | Based on | What it is | Main parameters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ssl.ClusterNet` | `ss.Network` | Fully connected clusters, such as households | `cluster_size`, `age_range`, `dynamic` |
| `ssl.HybridNet` | `ss.Network` | Covasim's households, schools, workplaces, and community | `household_size`, `contacts`, `beta`, `school_ages`, `work_ages` |
| `ssl.HouseholdNet` | `ss.Network` | Households built from survey data in the format of the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), optionally changing over time | `dhs_data`, `dynamic`, `prob_move_out` |
| `ssl.DiskNet` | `ss.Network` | People who move in a unit square, in contact with everyone within a radius | `r`, `v` |
| `ssl.StaticNet` | `ss.Network` | A fixed network from a NetworkX graph, or a function that makes one | `graph`, `p`, `n_contacts` |
| `ssl.ErdosRenyiNet` | `ss.DynamicNetwork` | Each pair of people connected with probability `p` at each step | `p`, `dur` |
| `ssl.RandomSafeNet` | `ss.DynamicNetwork` | Random contacts that stay the same for everyone else when people are added or removed, for comparing scenarios | `n_edges`, `dur` |
| `ssl.NullNet` | `ss.Network` | Each person in contact only with themselves, with no transmission, as a placeholder | none |

Like every network, these carry agents, so a model with one runs under the agent-based solver; [Contact networks](populations_networks.qmd) says how each would be approximated by a compartmental one. The tutorial [A2 – Networks](../tutorials/a2_networks.qmd) introduces networks with a worked example.

## Households and other clusters

Much transmission happens within households, schools, and workplaces: small groups whose members meet each other again and again. A random network with the same number of contacts spreads infection faster, because each contact is with someone new; in a household, an infectious person soon runs out of susceptible people to infect. `ssl.ClusterNet` divides people (optionally only those in `age_range`) into clusters of sizes drawn from `cluster_size` (by default Poisson with a mean of 4), with everyone in a cluster in contact with everyone else. Its contacts are made once, at the start (or redrawn every step, with `dynamic=True`).

Here the same SIR disease spreads with about 6 contacts per person: all of them random, or 1 random and the rest in households of about 6. With the same number of contacts, the households slow the epidemic, lower its peak, and leave more people never infected, since many of each person's contacts are already infected or immune. Each scenario is run 3 times, and the plot shows the median and the range:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl
ss.options(jupyter=True)

sir = lambda: ss.SIR(beta=ss.perday(0.05), dur_inf=ss.days(10), init_prev=0.005)
kw = dict(n_agents=2000, start='2000-01-01', dur=ss.days(200), dt=ss.days(1))
scenarios = {
    'Random contacts only': ss.Sim(diseases=sir(), networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=6), **kw),
    'Households and random contacts': ss.Sim(diseases=sir(), networks=[ssl.ClusterNet(cluster_size=ss.poisson(6)), ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=1)], **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, n_runs=3, parallel=False)
msim.plot(['sir.I', 'sir.R'])
```

`ssl.HybridNet` is the population of [Covasim](https://docs.covasim.org/): households (`h`, a `ClusterNet` with sizes drawn from a Poisson distribution with a mean of 2, as in Covasim, which gives about 2 contacts per person), schools for ages 6 to 22 (`s`), workplaces for ages 22 to 65 (`w`), and the community (`c`), each of the last three a random network with a Poisson number of contacts (`contacts`, by default 20, 16, and 20). When added to a sim, it becomes four networks, each reached by name and each with its own weight on transmission (`beta`, by default Covasim's 3, 0.6, 0.6, and 0.3), so that a contact at home counts for 10 times one in the community:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(diseases=ss.SIS(beta=ss.perday(0.002)), networks=ssl.HybridNet(), n_agents=2000, start='2000', dur=ss.days(100), dt=ss.days(1))
sim.run()
for name, net in sim.networks.items():
    print(name, 'contacts per person:', round(2*len(net) / sim.people.n_alive, 1))
sim.plot('sis')
```

To give the weight of each layer on the disease instead of the network, set the network's weights to 1 (`beta=dict(h=1, s=1, w=1, c=1)`) and give the disease one β per network: `ss.SIS(beta=dict(h=0.03, s=0.006, w=0.006, c=0.003))`. Each layer can be changed separately once the sim is made, for example by an intervention that closes schools by setting the weights of `sim.networks.s` to 0 (see [Interventions](interventions_interventions.qmd)).

### Households from survey data

`ssl.HouseholdNet` builds households from [DHS](https://dhsprogram.com) household survey data, setting each agent's age and sex to match a randomly drawn real household, so that the ages of the people living together are realistic (children with their parents, grandparents with both). With `dynamic=True` (the default), households also change: one woman is the head of each household, pregnant women other than the head may move out to form new households (with probability `prob_move_out`), and babies join their mother's household; this needs `ss.Pregnancy`.

Real DHS data requires registration, so `dhs_data='default'` makes synthetic data with the same structure, for demonstrations and testing:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(networks=ssl.HouseholdNet(dhs_data='default'), demographics=ss.Pregnancy(), start='2000', stop='2010', dt=ss.months(1), n_agents=2000)
sim.run()

net = sim.networks.householdnet # The sim's own copy of the network
hh_ids = net.household_ids[net.household_ids.notnan] # Unborn agents have no household
sizes = np.bincount(hh_ids.astype(int))
sizes = sizes[sizes > 0]
print('Households:', len(sizes))
print('Mean household size:', round(sizes.mean(), 1))
print('Largest household:', sizes.max())
```

To use real data, download a Household Recode (HR) dataset in Stata format, and load it with `HouseholdNet.load_dhs()`; any table with a household ID (`hh_id`) and the ages of its members as text (`ages`, such as `'72, 17, 30'`), and optionally their sexes (`sexes`, 1 for male and 2 for female), will also do:

```python
dhs_data = ssl.HouseholdNet.load_dhs('XXHR7xDT/XXHR7xFL.DTA')
sim = ss.Sim(networks=ssl.HouseholdNet(dhs_data=dhs_data))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`HouseholdNet` sets the age and sex of every agent (other than unborn agents) when it starts. Take care when using it with other modules that set or depend on age and sex, such as `ss.people('Kenya')` (see [People and agents](populations_people.qmd)).
:::

## Space

`ssl.DiskNet` is a spatial network: each agent has a position (`x`, `y`) in a unit square and a heading, moves at speed `v` each step (by default 0.05 a day), bounces off the walls, and is in contact with every agent within radius `r` (by default 0.1). Because contacts depend on position, an epidemic spreads outwards from each case as a wave, rather than evenly through the population. The positions are states of the network, so they can be plotted at any point in a run; here the sim runs in stages, with the agents moving slowly, and plots who is susceptible, infected, and recovered at each:

```{python}
sir = lambda: ss.SIR(beta=ss.perday(0.1), dur_inf=ss.days(10), init_prev=ss.choose_n(3))
kw = dict(n_agents=2000, start='2000-01-01', dur=ss.days(150), dt=ss.days(1))
disk = ss.Sim(diseases=sir(), networks=ssl.DiskNet(r=0.04, v=ss.freqperday(0.001)), **kw)

states = dict(S=('Susceptible', 'lightgray'), I=('Infected', 'tab:red'), R=('Recovered', 'tab:blue'))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4))
for ax, day in zip(axes, ['2000-01-31', '2000-03-01', '2000-04-15']):
    disk.run(until=day) # Run up to this day, then continue from here the next time
    net, sir_states = disk.networks.disknet, disk.diseases.sir
    for state, (label, color) in states.items():
        uids = getattr(sir_states, state).uids
        ax.scatter(net.x[uids], net.y[uids], s=4, color=color, label=label)
    ax.set_title(day)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
axes[0].legend(loc='lower left')
plt.show()
```

With a radius of 0.04, each agent has about 10 contacts (π × 0.04² × 2000). A random network with the same number of contacts gives a much faster, higher epidemic, since every contact can be anywhere:

```{python}
disk.run() # Finish the run
rand = ss.Sim(diseases=sir(), networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10), **kw).run()

fig = plt.figure()
plt.plot(disk.t.datevec, disk.results.sir.I, label='Spatial (ssl.DiskNet)')
plt.plot(rand.t.datevec, rand.results.sir.I, label='Random (ss.RandomNet)')
plt.ylabel('Number infected')
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

For movement between distinct places (villages, districts, countries) rather than continuous space, see [Geography](populations_geography.qmd).

## Theoretical networks

`ssl.StaticNet` makes a fixed network from a [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) graph: either a graph made beforehand, with one node for each agent, or a function that makes one, given with its arguments (`n`, the number of nodes, is filled in, and `seed=True` uses the sim's random numbers). It is the way to use any of the many graphs that NetworkX can make: small-world, scale-free, regular, and so on. Here a small-world graph (Watts–Strogatz: each person in contact with their 10 nearest neighbors on a ring, with 5% of contacts rewired at random) is compared with a random regular graph, in which each person also has exactly 10 contacts but anywhere:

```{python}
import networkx as nx

sir = lambda: ss.SIR(beta=ss.perday(0.05), dur_inf=ss.days(10), init_prev=0.005)
kw = dict(n_agents=2000, start='2000-01-01', dur=ss.days(200), dt=ss.days(1))
scenarios = {
    'Small world': ss.Sim(diseases=sir(), networks=ssl.StaticNet(graph=nx.watts_strogatz_graph, k=10, p=0.05), **kw),
    'Random regular': ss.Sim(diseases=sir(), networks=ssl.StaticNet(graph=nx.random_regular_graph, d=10), **kw),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, parallel=False)
msim.plot('sir.I')
```

The small world's clustering (a person's contacts are also each other's) slows the epidemic and lowers its peak, though nearly everyone is infected in both.

The other three are for theory, testing, and development:

- `ssl.ErdosRenyiNet` is the classic random graph: each possible pair of people is connected with probability `p` (by default 0.1) at each step, so each person's number of contacts is binomial, with a mean of `p` times the population. It is useful for comparison with analytic results; for random mixing in general, `ss.RandomNet` is much faster, since it doesn't consider every pair. With `dur` greater than 0, contacts last, and new ones keep accumulating.
- `ssl.RandomSafeNet` is a random network written so that each agent's contacts depend only on that agent's own random numbers (see [Random numbers](mechanics_random.qmd)). Adding or removing people then changes the contacts of only a few others, which keeps differences between scenarios down to the scenarios rather than chance. Each agent has `n_edges` edges (so about twice as many contacts); it is slower than `ss.RandomNet`.
- `ssl.NullNet` connects each agent only to themselves, with a weight of 0, so it never transmits. It is a placeholder while developing a model whose real network isn't written yet, or for testing a disease's natural history alone.

To see what random-number safety means for a network, make the same network for 1,000 and 1,001 agents, and count how many of the contacts among the first 1,000 survive the extra person:

```{python}
def contacts(net, n_agents):
    """ The contacts among the first 1,000 agents after one step, as a set of pairs """
    sim = ss.Sim(networks=net, n_agents=n_agents, start='2000-01-01', dur=ss.days(1), dt=ss.days(1), verbose=0)
    sim.run()
    edges = sim.networks[0].to_df()
    edges = edges[(edges.p1 < 1000) & (edges.p2 < 1000)]
    return set(zip(np.minimum(edges.p1, edges.p2), np.maximum(edges.p1, edges.p2)))

networks = {
    'ss.RandomNet': lambda: ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10),
    'ss.RandomNet (exact)': lambda: ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10, method='exact'),
    'ssl.RandomSafeNet': lambda: ssl.RandomSafeNet(n_edges=5),
}
for label, net in networks.items():
    before = contacts(net(), 1000)
    after = contacts(net(), 1001)
    print(label, 'contacts kept (%):', round(100*len(before & after)/len(before)))
```

One extra person changes about half of the contacts made by the default `ss.RandomNet`, nearly all of those made by `ss.RandomNet(method='exact')`, and almost none of those made by `ssl.RandomSafeNet`. For comparing scenarios that add or remove people (births, deaths, migration), the safe network keeps the comparison sharp; for everything else, `ss.RandomNet` is faster.

## Further reading

- [NetworkX: graph generators](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/generators.html): the graphs that `ssl.StaticNet` can use
- [EpiModel: network modeling for epidemics](https://www.epimodel.org/): epidemics on dynamic networks estimated from data (exponential random graph models)
- [Covasim: tutorial on people and networks](https://docs.covasim.org/tutorials/tut_people.html): the hybrid population that `ssl.HybridNet` comes from
- [DHS Program: data](https://dhsprogram.com/data/): the household surveys that `ssl.HouseholdNet` reads
- [Mesa: agent-based modeling in Python](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/): agents in space and on networks, more generally
